narrative: The wildfire was human caused and started near the intersection of Colockum Road and Tarpiscan Road. The fire spread south into neighboring Kittitas County and remained west of the Columbia River. The fire continued to burn into the month of August. Numerous homes, three major power lines, a natural gas line, two wind farms, timber, water quality, wildlife habitat and range resources were all threatened at one point or another. Three primary residences and several outbuildings were burned. Two fire fighters suffered minor injuries.

zone: SAN BERNARDINO AND RIVERSIDE COUNTY VALLEYS - THE INLAND EMPIRE
narrative: The Etiwanda fire began on April 30th around 0700 PST in the San Bernardino National Forest near Rancho Cucamonga in San Bernardino County. The fire was due to an escaped illegal campfire a few days prior, when strong winds blew embers that ignited in Day Canyon. A mandatory evacuation order was issued for Rancho Cucamonga residents from Haven Avenue to Carnelian Street, north of Hillside Road, as well as the area West of Etiwanda, North of Wilson and East of Day Creek Wash. Schools evacuated included Day Creek Intermediate School, Los Osos High School, Heritage Intermediate School and Caryn Elementary. The fire burned rapidly south, threatening 600-800 structures. 2143 acres before being fully contained on May 6. Three firefighters sustained unknown minor injuries and one structure was damaged.

The lightning-caused fire, which began July 14, blackened 269,186 acres; leveled approximately 325 homes, 146 barns, outbuildings and fences; damaged utilities, killed cattle, wildlife and other livestock, and destroyed or damaged orchards, crops, forest and range land. Total cost to fight the fire was approximately 87 million dollars.  The fire spanned two different public zones and cost and acreage is highly uncertain per zone.

The Hunters wildfire was managed by CalFire. Ignition was 5/26/14 and the cause was unknown. The location was 5 miles south of Coulterville, CA (Mariposa County) and the size was 677 acres. Containment was reached on 6/2 and the cost to containment was $4.4 Million. There were two residences lost and one outbuilding. There were no fatalities and unknown injuries.

The Chiwaukum Complex started from a lightning strike on July 14th but did not erupt until July 15th at approximately 0600 PST. The complex of fires burned 50,540 acres. 543 homes were threatened over the 45 day period but none were lost. Four other structures were burned including one outbuilding and three seasonal cabins. The approximate cost for fighting the fire was 38 million dollars. The Chiwaukum Creek Fire burned 13,895 acres; Alpine Fire burned 19 acres; Kelly Mountain Fire burned 124 acres; Shoofly Fire burned 163 acres; Mills Canyon Fire burned 22,571 acres; Hansel Creek Fire burned 1,073 acres; Duncan Fire burned 12,695 acres north of Entiat, WA.

The Tokewanna Fire was discovered on the afternoon of July 28, about 15 miles south of Mountain View, Wyoming. The fire burned approximately 1,300 acres and destroyed 8 structures in the Tokewanna Estates Subdivision. The fire forced the evacuation of 140 homes and the Uinta County Youth Camp, and also closed portions of Highways 271 and 410. One firefighter on the wildfire suffered burns from the fire. The fire was 100% contained as of 6 p.m. MDT Saturday, August 6.

In the early morning hours of October 16th, lightning ignited a wildfire deep in the heart of the Cohutta Wilderness in the Chattahoochee National Forest. The ���Rough Ridge��� wildfire spread through the very remote Cohutta Wilderness and surrounding portions of the Chattahoochee National Forest, eventually consuming 27,950 acres in Fannin, Gilmer and Murray Counties. Nearly $8.5 million federal dollars were expended fighting this wildfire before it was finally declared contained on November 30th.

A structure caught on fire and spread to nearby vegetation. 412 acres were burned about five miles west-southwest of Durango. The Brianhead Fire started on June 17, when a man used a weed torch at his Brian Head area cabin, and the fire became out of control. The fire burned 71,672 acres, with most of the growth in the first two weeks of the fire. The Brianhead Fire destroyed 13 homes and 13 minor structures. A priority sage grouse habitat was also impacted east of the fire perimeter in the Panguitch watershed area. Costs associated with the fire were approximately $36.6 million, with rehabilitation efforts projected to cost double or triple that amount. At the height of the fire, approximately 1,831 personnel were fighting to contain the wildfire, and 1,562 people were evacuated from 11 communities in Iron and Garfield counties. The fire was contained on July 28. Note that this event began in June.

narrative: The Horse Park Fire began at the end of May during a lightning event 15 miles southwest of Norwood and continued to expand to a total of 1,221 acres before it was contained.  A resource truck got stuck and firefighters were forced to abandon it. The truck was later consumed by the fire.

zone: GORE AND ELK MOUNTAINS/CENTRAL MOUNTAIN VALLEYS
narrative: The Lake Christine fire began in early July from human causes, allegedly from tracer rounds fired at the Basalt Gun Range about mile northwest of Basalt. Lack of rainfall and gusty winds allowed the fire to grow to a total of 12,588 acres before it was finally contained in the beginning of October. Periodic road closures were in effect as well as closures in the White River National Forest. Numerous neighborhoods were evacuated. The fire destroyed three homes, a barn and an outbuilding. The three homes had a combined value of $2.65 million.

The Dollar Ridge Fire was a human caused wildfire that began during the afternoon of July 1. The fire burned 68,869 acres and destroyed 363 structures, including 74 homes. Costs to fight the fire were approximately $18 million, though rehabilitation efforts were projected to add significantly to the cost. At the height of the fire, approximately 1,100 people were evacuated from communities in Wasatch and Duchesne Counties. The fire was considered effectively contained on August 31, at 94% containment. Note that this event began in July.
